q: Should I split purchases into production and non-production when building Category 1?
title: Production vs non-production purchases
short: It is optional, and usually worth doing. The GHG Protocol says splitting purchases into production-related items (materials, components, parts) and non-production items (office supplies, IT support, services) can follow how your purchase team already buys, which makes the data easier to organise and collect.
audience: Manufacturers and exporters building a first Category 1 estimate

p: Box 5.2 of the Scope 3 Standard draws the line like this:
ul: Production-related (often called direct procurement): materials, components and parts you process or build into your product; goods bought for resale, for traders and distributors only; and plant and equipment used to make the product.

Non-production-related (often called indirect procurement): office supplies, furniture, computers, phones, travel services, IT support, outsourced admin, consulting, housekeeping and gardening; plus maintenance, repair and operations items such as spare parts.

sections.h: The split organises data; it does not change categories
p: Category 1 holds every purchase not reported in Categories 2 to 8. So machines and other capital goods still go to Category 2, upstream fuel and power losses to Category 3, freight you pay for to Category 4 and travel to Category 6, whichever side of the split they sit on.

ul: Production purchases are usually a few vendors with tonnes or kilograms printed on the invoice: steel, granules, yarn, cartons. These suit quantity-based factors or supplier data.
Non-production purchases are many small vendors billed by value. A spend-based estimate is usually enough.
The Technical Guidance allows different methods for different activities within one category, so each side can use the method that fits it.

sections.h: How to split your purchase register
ol: Raw material and packing material ledgers: production-related. Cartons and pallets that leave with your product count here.
Consumables, stationery, AMC, repairs, professional fees: non-production.
Spare parts for machines: non-production, as maintenance, repair and operations, even though they are used on the shop floor.
Check doubtful lines by HSN code, then keep the rule the same every year.

p: Many companies start with production purchases only. The Scope 3 Standard uses this exact case as an example: adding non-production procurement to Category 1 in a later year is a change in activities that can trigger a base year recalculation if the effect is significant. Note what you left out in year one so the change is easy to explain.

example.title: Illustration: a Ludhiana fastener maker's purchases for one year
lines: Plating chemicals: Rs 0.9 crore; cartons: Rs 0.6 crore (production)
Total Rs 17.4 crore; production side 15.9 / 17.4 = 91% of spend from a handful of vendors, with tonnes on the invoice
Plan: quantity-based or supplier data for wire rod first; spend-based for the 140 small vendors

senseible: Senseible reads purchase invoices line by line with HSN code, quantity and unit, and keeps Scope 3 lines in a separate supplier evidence trail, so you can sort production materials from consumables before choosing a method for each.
